storylines.title: They trailed in every game of the series. They swept it anyway
storylines.observation: The Milwaukee Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLCS for their first pennant since 1982, then took Game 1 of the World Series 3-2 over Tampa Bay - a franchise that has never won a title facing one that hasn't either.
storylines.question: What does it mean to win every game of a series without ever actually being ahead until the moment that mattered?
storylines.hidden_question: Does a result like this reveal something real about a team's character, or is it just the kind of statistical oddity that looks meaningful only in hindsight?
storylines.pattern: a decisive, clean-looking outcome built out of narrow, late comebacks rather than sustained dominance
storylines.why_now: Game 2 made the pattern impossible to miss: down 4-0 in the first inning, Milwaukee tied it on a Sal Frelick homer in the sixth, took the lead in the seventh, and closed it out 5-4 - a second straight win manufactured entirely in the back half of the game, now a 2-0 series lead.
storylines.season_or_time_context: World Series Game 1 played Oct 23, 2026; Game 2 Oct 24

history.note: Game 2: Brewers 5, Rays 4. Tampa Bay scored four in the top of the first; Milwaukee tied it on Sal Frelick's sixth-inning homer, took the lead in the seventh on a Cooper Pratt RBI, and closed it out - a 2-0 series lead built from another come-from-behind win.

Game 1: Brewers 3, Rays 2. Milwaukee scored twice in the first on balls that clanked off Tampa Bay gloves, then survived a bases-loaded ninth when a reversed replay call turned a potential double play into a run-scoring groundout before Trevor Megill closed it out anyway.

Game 1 is tonight in Milwaukee. Tampa Bay's two scheduled starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, both made their MLB debuts with the Brewers - the team they're now trying to beat for a title neither franchise has ever won.
